steps.observation: Work on this for 10 seconds; do not stop early. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Key differences between DNA and RNA

Chemical composition  
• Sugar: DNA contains deoxyribose (lacking an ‑OH on the 2′ carbon); RNA contains ribose (has the 2′-OH).  
• Nitrogenous bases: DNA uses thymine (T); RNA uses uracil (U) in place of thymine.  
• Overall stability: The 2′-OH in RNA makes the phosphodiester backbone more prone to hydrolysis; DNA is chemically more stable.

Strandedness and structure  
• DNA is typically double-stranded, forming the well-known antiparallel double helix.  
• RNA is usually single-stranded, but it can fold back on itself to create hairpins, stem-loops and complex 3-D shapes (tRNA, rRNA, ribozymes).  
• Length: Genomic DNA can be millions of base pairs long; individual RNA molecules are usually far shorter (tens to thousands of bases).

Cellular roles  
• DNA serves primarily as the long-term genetic repository.  
• RNA serves multiple, more transient roles:  
  – mRNA carries protein-coding information from DNA to ribosomes.  
  – rRNA forms the catalytic core of ribosomes.  
  – tRNA delivers amino acids during translation.  
  – Regulatory RNAs (miRNA, siRNA, lncRNA, etc.) modulate gene expression.  
  – Some RNA molecules (ribozymes, spliceosomal RNAs) exhibit enzymatic activity.

Localization and lifespan  
• DNA resides mainly in the nucleus (and mitochondria/chloroplasts) and persists for the life of the cell.  
• RNA is synthesized in the nucleus (or organelles) but many species function in the cytoplasm; most have short half-lives, turning over quickly.

Replication vs. transcription  
• DNA is copied by DNA polymerases during S phase, using both strands as templates.  
• RNA is synthesized by RNA polymerases during transcription, using only one DNA strand as template.

Repair and proofreading  
• DNA repair pathways (NER, BER, MMR, HR, NHEJ) maintain genomic integrity.  
• RNA, being transient, lacks comparable proofreading/repair; erroneous RNAs are usually degraded.

Chemical modifications  
• DNA modifications are mostly limited to cytosine (5-methyl-C) and, in some organisms, adenine (6-methyl-A).  
• RNA undergoes diverse modifications (pseudouridine, methylations, editing) that fine-tune structure and function.

Functional consequences  
• The extra ‑OH in RNA enables catalysis and intricate folding, supporting roles in splicing, peptide-bond formation, and regulation.  
• DNA’s stability and double-strandedness make it ideal for long-term information storage and accurate replication.

In short: DNA is the durable, double-stranded genetic archive; RNA is the versatile, generally single-stranded molecule that interprets, regulates and sometimes catalyzes that genetic information.
